I am fifty years old and have farmed this land for thirty years. I never went to school, but I know every corner of my 10.9 mu. My household has six people and some of them work in factories in town, so I cannot take risks or try new crops I do not understand. Here in Quzhou, every family grows winter wheat followed by summer maize on the same fields — that is what the land knows, what the buyers want, and what I have always done.

It is autumn now. After I harvest the summer maize, I will run the rotary tiller over all 10.9 mu to chop the stalks and loosen the soil. Then I will sow winter wheat in early October. I will buy improved wheat seed from the village co-op — Jimai 22 or Luyuan 502, the kinds my neighbors plant. Before sowing I spread compound fertilizer as base dressing, and in spring when the wheat turns green I top-dress with urea. I irrigate three times from my well: once after sowing, once at jointing in April, and once at heading in May. I spray herbicide once in early spring, insecticide once for aphids, and if I see rust I spray fungicide too.

In early June, as soon as the wheat is cut, I will plant summer maize immediately. I will not till — I direct-seed into the wheat stubble to save diesel and time, because the maize season is short. I buy hybrid seed from the shop, Denghai 605 or Zhengdan 958. I put down compound fertilizer at planting and side-dress urea when the maize is knee-high. Summer brings rain, so I only irrigate twice: once at sowing if the soil is dry, and once at silking if July turns hot. I spray herbicide after emergence and insecticide once for corn borer.

I expect about 450 kg per mu of wheat and 550 kg per mu of maize. That is what I usually get, and I do not gamble with the harvest. My family needs the grain money, and the grain station still buys wheat and maize without trouble.
